analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital stay after a mastectomy.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 197 cosponsors from both parties, but no committee ever voted on it and it died without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group and individual health insurance plans to pay for at least 48 hours in the hospital after a mastectomy and 24 hours after lymph node surgery for breast cancer. Insurers and plans could not pressure women to leave early with cash rebates, could not penalize doctors who kept patients in the hospital, and could not force doctors to get sign-off for the stay. Women who wanted to go home sooner, with their doctor's agreement, still could.
analysis.who_benefits: Women facing breast cancer surgery, who would have had a floor of paid hospital recovery time instead of insurer-decided short stays, and hospitals and doctors, who would be paid for that time rather than pushed to discharge patients early.

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and insurers from covering less than 48 hours after a mastectomy or less than 24 hours after a lymph node dissection, and from requiring advance authorization for the stay [S2].
Prohibits plans from paying women cash to accept a shorter stay, from denying coverage to dodge the rules, and from penalizing or enticing doctors to discharge patients early [S2].
Lets a woman leave earlier if her attending doctor, in consultation with her, decides to [S3].
Applies the same minimum to individual-market insurance, and leaves stricter state laws in place rather than overriding them [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Group health plans and insurers pay for longer stays, and employers who fund plans, especially self-insured employers under ERISA, would bear much of that added cost, passed along in premiums. Critics of benefit mandates argued these requirements raise everyone's premiums.

drawbacks.text: Mandated hospital stays add to the cost of coverage, and those costs flow to employers and premium payers; the bill leaves insurers free to keep charging deductibles and coinsurance, just at a rate that cannot increase during the required stay [S3].
Many states already had their own minimum-stay laws, and for those states the bill would change little, since it does not override stricter state requirements [S2].
A federal 48-hour floor, even with a doctor-and-patient exception, is a blunt tool compared with leaving the length of stay entirely to medical judgment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women facing mastectomy, the benefit is direct and concrete: paid recovery time in the hospital instead of a coverage rule that pushed early discharge. The cost is higher premiums spread across all enrollees, and the number of women affected in any year is small compared with the whole insured population. It is a real but targeted benefit, and the bill was written narrowly, with an opt-out for early discharge and respect for stricter state laws.

outcome.mechanism: Both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee referred it to subcommittees, no subcommittee or full committee ever acted, and the bill expired at the end of the Congress without a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on February 8, 2001, with 99 original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce, then split between their health subcommittees in March 2001 [S5].
By the end of the Congress it had 197 cosponsors, including 170 of 208 House Democrats and 26 of 223 House Republicans [S4].
No markup, vote, or further action ever appears in the bill's action history after the subcommittee referrals in March 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and self-insured employers kept the ability to limit post-mastectomy stays and avoid the added cost of mandated recovery time; the 197 cosponsors got credit for supporting a bill that never had to become law.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily bipartisan in total numbers, though weighted toward Democrats: 170 of 208 House Democrats and 26 of 223 House Republicans signed on, with no recorded votes because none ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill forced insurers to pay for at least 48 hours of post-mastectomy stay and stopped them from paying patients cash to leave early or pressuring doctors to discharge sooner. That cost them a tool for holding down claim costs.
Plans funded by employers directly fall under the ERISA section of the bill, so employers would have absorbed much of the added cost of longer stays.
Longer covered stays mean more paid inpatient days for breast cancer surgery patients; the bill also barred plans from cutting provider reimbursement for following the rules.
